items.title: The Wisdom of Water: Alan Watts on the Ocean and the Meaning of Life
items.description: Four billion years ago, in the hydrothermal vents at the bottom of the world where serpentine is forged, chemistry trembled with the promise of consciousness and matter began its long metabolic pilgrimage toward mind. Perhaps our saline cells remember it: how we, pilgrims of the possible, crawled out of the tide pools to climb the trees, then came down from the trees to live under a canopy of one hundred trillion synapses animated by the oceanic yearning to make meaning of our mortality. items.title: Anaïs Nin on Why Emotional Excess is Essential to Creativity
items.description: "Something is always born of excess: great art was born of great terrors, great loneliness, great inhibitions, instabilities, and it always balances them."

items.title: Yes to Life, in Spite of Everything: Viktor Frankl’s Lost Lectures on Moving Beyond Optimism and Pessimism to Find the Deepest Source of Meaning
items.description: "Everything depends on the individual human being, regardless of how small a number of like-minded people there is... on each person... creatively making the meaning of life a reality in his or her own being."

items.title: How to Be a Good Explorer on the Lifelong Expedition to Yourself
items.description: Life is an ongoing expedition into the brambled tendrilled wilderness of ourselves, continually stymied by all we mistake for a final destination — success, superhuman strength, the love of another. Along the way, we keep confusing experiment and exploration. An experiment proves or disproves an existing theory; its payoff is data, fixed and binary. items.title: Hannah Arendt on Love and How to Live with the Fundamental Fear of Loss
items.description: “Fearlessness is what love seeks… Such fearlessness exists only in the complete calm that can no longer be shaken by events expected of the future… Hence the only valid tense is the present, the Now.”

items.title: How to Hold What Harrows You
items.description: We are shaped by all we have suffered — by what harrows us — and in turn shape our lives by how we hold our harrowing. Harrow shares its Middle English root with harvest. It is by suffering, and by what we make of our suffering, that our personhood ripens in us, that we come to reap what evolution sowed long ago when mitochondria first set out to become mind — our capacity for empathy, for doubt, for art. items.title: J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”
items.description: "Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds."

items.title: The Stoic Antidote to Frustration: Marcus Aurelius on How to Keep Your Mental Composure and Emotional Equanimity When People Let You Down
items.description: The art of tempering your fury with an infuriating existential truth.

items.title: Swimming and the Meaning of Life
items.description: One of my earliest and most vivid childhood memories is of swimming in a cool pool bounded by boulders in the middle of a river in the mountains of Bulgaria, the late-afternoon sun casting komorebi on the water through the rustling leaves. I can still hear the feeling-tone in my body, the strange and lovely simultaneity of absolute presence and absolute peace. I didn’t yet know the word for transcendence. items.title: Thank You, Everything: An Illustrated Love Letter to the World
items.description: We forget that none of this had to exist — that we weren’t owed mountains and music by the universe. And maybe we have to forget — or we would be too stupefied with gratitude for every raindrop and every eyelash to get through the daily tasks punctuating the unbidden wonder of our lives. items.title: Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing
items.description: "Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time."

items.title: Kurt Vonnegut’s 8 Tenets of Storytelling
items.description: "Write to please just one person. If you open a window and make love to the world, so to speak, your story will get pneumonia."

items.title: Nick Cave on the Two Pillars of a Meaningful Life
items.description: "Cultivating a questioning mind, of which conversation is the chief instrument, enriches our relationship with the world."

items.title: The Story Behind Dylan Thomas’s “Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night” and the Poet’s Own Stirring Reading of His Masterpiece
items.description: "Rage, rage against the dying of the light."

items.title: A Spell Against Stagnation: John O’Donohue on Beginnings
items.description: "Our very life here depends directly on continuous acts of beginning."
